dataset.title: DATASETS HEATSHIELD project Loughborough University, averaged per condition and individual sessions
dataset.funding: HEAT-SHIELD, European Union Horizon 2020 grant agreement 668786

source_file.name: D2 DATASET FINAL HEATSHIELD individual sessions March 2024 PWC6.xlsx

derived_slice.selection: Rows from source studies 1 through 6 only. The workbook explanation identifies studies 1-6 as the complete one-hour modelling trials and studies 7-14 as duplicate subsets created for within-subject comparisons.
derived_slice.transformation: Selected and renamed twelve source columns; normalized YES/NO solar and coverall flags to true/false; retained source numeric precision; did not impute, alter, or generate measurements.

fields.study_id: Source study number; studies 1-6 are the non-duplicate one-hour trial groups.
fields.participant_id: Pseudonymous participant identifier from the public source workbook.
fields.air_temperature_c: Measured average air temperature in degrees Celsius.
fields.relative_humidity_percent: Measured average relative humidity in percent.
fields.air_speed_mps: Measured average air speed in metres per second.
fields.solar_exposure: Whether the experimental solar-radiation condition was active.
fields.high_clothing_coverage: Whether the participant wore the high-coverage ensemble including a full-body coverall.
fields.apparent_temperature_c: Apparent Temperature calculated in the source workbook.
fields.heat_index_c: Heat Index in degrees Celsius calculated in the source workbook.
fields.wbgt_outdoor_c: Outdoor Wet Bulb Globe Temperature in degrees Celsius from the source workbook.
fields.utci_c: Universal Thermal Climate Index in degrees Celsius calculated in the source workbook.
fields.measured_pwc_loss_percent: Observed one-hour physical work capacity loss relative to the participant's thermoneutral reference condition.

required_attribution.title: An advanced empirical model for quantifying the impact of heat and climate change on human physical work capacity

Quantifying the impact of heat on human physical work capacity; part II: the observed interaction of air velocity with temperature, humidity, sweat rate, and clothing is not captured by most heat stress indices
Quantifying the impact of heat on human physical work capacity; part III: the impact of solar radiation varies with air temperature, humidity, and clothing coverage
Quantifying the impact of heat on human physical work capacity; part IV: interactions between work duration and heat stress severity
Comparing the efficacy of different climate indices for prediction of labor loss, body temperatures, and thermal perception in a wide variety of warm and hot climates

limitations: These are controlled environmental-chamber exercise trials, not observations from the fictional Phoenix logistics yard.
The outcome is measured physical work capacity loss, not heat illness, injury, or a regulatory compliance result.
Participants contributed repeated trials, so records are not statistically independent; HeatShift reports descriptive correlations without inferential p-values.
The public slice does not contain workplace schedules, real employer data, worker identities, acclimatization status, or on-site Phoenix WBGT measurements.
HeatShift applies a fixed benchmark profile and does not fit or tune policy thresholds on these measurements.
